Merewash lies below a stony northern rise, above old salt lenses, and around clay channels that carry sudden water but crack open in long drought. Its surviving wells are deepest west of the settlement. A proposed course should therefore be tested for four questions:

1. **Where does the first water fall?** The fall must be enough to move, but not so steep that it cuts directly through inhabited clay.
2. **Where is water held?** The course needs one seasonal storage reach above the settlement or within deep compatible ground.
3. **What ground receives it?** A course associated only with peat, ice, or fresh volcanic soil may be accurate and still unsuitable.
4. **Where does excess go?** The course needs an overflow that does not run through Merewash's central fields and houses.

A course does not have to reproduce an old river exactly. The fungal current supplies a tendency: a sequence of gradients, storage behaviors, ground associations, and overflow responses around which the rain-seed can organize its first watershed.

### Living braid

The most reliable method is to bring three or more compatible cord families into one wet braid without cutting them from their surrounding network. Route a measured rain feed through the chosen strands, keep incompatible branches physically separate, and carry the joined outflow toward a crownward root channel.

- **Requirements:** working warm rain, at least four compatible measure families, a continuous living path, and someone checking the source and the crownward receiver.
- **Visible result:** the braid repeats shorter and shorter fragments until only distances, gradients, ground signs, and overflow intervals remain. A pale pulse travels crownward through the outflow.
- **Persistent cost:** the selected branch becomes temporarily quiet behind the transfer and cannot support another full course during this migration.
- **Later option:** the crown can organize a weather-knot around a working river tendency, and Nahl can defend why that tendency suits Merewash.

### Wet transcription

Copy stable measurements onto a board, cord gauge, marked pipe, knotted line, or field sheet while the branch remains alive.

- **Requirements:** patient comparison and at least two independent repetitions of each copied feature.
- **Visible result:** the record stays intelligible after the voice changes.
- **Persistent cost:** transcription consumes time and may miss a late-opening family.
- **Later option:** Merewash receives a human-readable record even if no seed is taken. The copy does not itself supply the living memory current to the crown.

### Cut living branch

A cord can be cut and carried wet, but severing it strips away neighboring relations.

- **Requirements:** a sealed wet wrap and a clear choice about which family is being sacrificed.
- **Visible result:** the cut branch repeats one short sequence with great clarity, then begins substituting voice and interval.
- **Persistent cost:** the source family is broken and the carried current is weak at best.
- **Later option:** a difficult route can still carry partial course evidence, but the crown may form a smaller or unstable watershed pattern.

### Flood the hollow

Opening several basin feeds at once wakes almost every cord.

- **Visible result:** the hollow becomes loud enough to feel through bone and root; many valid measures overlap with incompatible courses.
- **Persistent cost:** warm rain pools instead of returning, distinctions wash out, and the cords may remain weak after drainage.
- **Later option:** Several historic courses become undeniable, while selection becomes slower and less precise. Flooding is no shortcut to a perfect answer.

## Current states

Record the remembered river course as one of the six ecological current states.

- **Absent:** no living selected branch reaches the crown, or all available branches have been dried, scorched, severed, or mixed beyond distinction.
- **Weak:** a stable fall and ground relation reach the crown, but storage or overflow remains missing, contradictory, or dependent on a severed branch.
- **Working:** coherent fall, storage, ground, and overflow relations travel through a living wet path to the crown.
- **Strong:** the working course also has interval confirmation, a redundant compatible family, or a complete human transcription. It can absorb one later strain such as a shortened transfer or one damaged strand.

A strong memory current cannot replace absent rain. The cords require living circulation to speak and to transfer their pattern.

## People in the hollow

**Nahl Reed** listens for fall, storage, ground, overflow, and interval. A voice may be beautiful, familiar, and wrong for Merewash. Nahl says so without calling the voice false.

**Sio Tern** recognizes inherited counting cadences and becomes most careful when the words seem intimate. If the measure persists while the kinship changes, Sio treats the measure as evidence and the kinship as drift.

**Hessa Clay** may hear Tovan's fresh roster call before he reaches camp. Once Tovan is safe, she can place the living man and the repeated work side by side: the cord kept how he called, not the person who called.

**Jun Alder** hears proof that useful observation can outlive its maker and its country. That may make the eastward road imaginable. It does not make it chosen.

A player character may hear a familiar cadence. Ask for one practical thing that person repeated—a flood mark, a well depth, a weather sign, a field boundary, a road interval. Keep the observation. Let private detail drift. The hollow has no final message to deliver.

## Complications and failure-forward consequences

- A selected course is accurate but associated with ground unlike Merewash. The party must seek another family or accept a weak current.
- A wet branch crosses the safest return route. Preserving the living transfer makes movement harder rather than impossible.
- A character follows a familiar voice into a tightening cord loop. Rescue may break one strand, delay selection, or require another person to hold the route.
- Fire heat reaches an outer cord. The party can cool the edge, sacrifice the affected family, or move the selected braid sooner.
- Flooded voices produce two plausible overflows. The party can compare interval evidence, copy both for Merewash, or choose one and record the uncertainty.
- A cut branch remains clear enough to use but cannot carry all four required relationships. It creates a weak course rather than no course.

Leave a legible record of what remains true. A mistaken choice alters the course; it does not summon an unrelated curse or a lying ghost.

## Stage changes

- **Long Shade:** one voice at a time can be distinguished, but several important families remain dry.
- **Red Dusk:** warm rain exposes the network and allows careful cross-comparison.
- **Root Night:** course relations become vivid, personal details blur quickly, and the living braid can reach the descending crown.
- **Glass Dawn:** outer cords dry and crack. A course already transferred remains; an unselected course becomes inaccessible from ordinary routes.

## Results and later options

Record more than “the voices are not ghosts”:

- which measure families were observed;
- which familiar voices appeared and what practical observation each carried;
- which present-tense or flow test demonstrated the hollow's limits;
- which course was selected and why it suits Merewash;
- whether the transfer path is absent, weak, working, or strong;
- what warm rain was returned, pooled, spent, or fouled;
- whether a human transcription survives; and
- which route remains open from the hollow toward the chamber, crown, or exit.

The hollow offers evidence, a living course, and difficult grief—never permission from the dead.

## Late access and moving evidence

After the outer cords become inaccessible, only a living braid already connected to water or a surviving transcription carries the selected course westward. The living braid can supply the remembered-course current. A transcription preserves measured fall, storage, ground, overflow, and interval relations as evidence and a construction template, but it is not itself living memory.

A clue heard through a carried braid remains sourced to the Hollow of Kept Voices. Personal details that washed out near dawn cannot be reconstructed from the stable measurements, and a late cadence does not become a whole person merely because it is emotionally recognizable.

encounters.title: Blackgrass Burn
encounters.summary: A low renewal fire must cross the wagon scar, repaired soil corridor, and crownward seam without taking a second road through oil, canvas, pollen, or people.
encounters.opening_view: The blackgrass whitens first. Then a low red line runs the old scar, opening seed shells without smoking—until blue flame leaps sideways into spilled spice. Canvas tightens in the heat. Lantern pollen burns gold above it. On one flank, returned basin water beads on black living soil; on the other, fire reaches the forked wagons. The next gust comes from the Bearer’s vents.
encounters.content:
## Situation

Blackgrass grows in narrow bands along an old scar across the Bearer's upper roots. Its blades remain matte and cool until heat nears; then they whiten from tip to base, curl away from living margins, and kindle in a low advancing front. Behind it, hard shells open, parasites die, and young roots find a cleared seam.

The front reaches the wagon scar during Red Dusk. There it meets oil, spice dust, loose grain, torn canvas, animal hair, dry fungus, and lantern pollen—each a possible road the old burn never meant to follow. Smother every blade and the crown coats remain sealed. Let every flame run and the repaired soil route, chosen fungal braid, captured dawn, or trapped people may burn with it.

Make the fire legible: fuel, two margins, living-soil breaks, vent wind, intended receiver, and at least two ways out. “Necessary” does not mean “benign,” and a runaway front is never a stronger form of the same current.

## What the fire does

A working heat current performs three related tasks in order:

1. **Renew the migration corridor.** The narrow front burns parasites and dead sheath above living soil without baking the delivered old ground.
2. **Open prepared coats.** Heat reaches crownward shells only after soil, light, rain, and river course have begun to fill them.
3. **Clear flexible root growth.** The old scar guides fire across tissue that can regrow behind it.

Heat too early opens empty shells that collapse. Heat too late leaves complete but sealed knots that travel east. Heat outside the scar consumes dependencies rather than completing them.

Cut blackgrass dries and burns hotter. A carried ember can extend a prepared path; it cannot replace the continuous living corridor and its margins.

## Reading the front

Before intervening, establish five physical facts.

1. **Leading edge:** where blades are whitening but not yet burning.
2. **Left margin:** what living tissue, wet line, old soil, or bare mineral keeps flame from spreading.
3. **Right margin:** the second independent boundary. One sound edge does not make a bounded corridor.
4. **Receiver:** which renewal scar, prepared shell path, or crownward seam the heat is meant to reach.
5. **Escape route:** where people and animals can move if wind, pollen, or reflected heat changes the front.

Then identify exceptional fuels: oil, spice dust, dry canvas, loose grain chaff, cut lantern stems, animal bedding, resinous wood, or spilled lamp wick. State which are inside the corridor, which lie across a margin, and which can be removed only by abandoning useful cargo.

A clear inspection reveals the front's behavior. Use a system check for time, a concealed oil run, or reaching a threatened load without exposure.

## The three burn segments

The fire crosses three distinct segments. Work in one may help another; resolve each segment on its own fuel, margins, and receiver.

### Wagon scar

The first segment runs through the place where the upper wagon crushed the soilbearer road. Spilled oil follows one root seam; spice dust lies across another. The fire must cross enough of the old scar to renew it without following either contaminant into the restored road or wagon pocket.

- **Primary problem:** exceptional fuel and trapped salvage.
- **Useful boundaries:** dark living soil, damp root flesh, cleared mineral fittings, and a returned basin gutter.
- **Common choice:** preserve intact wagon material or dismantle it to remove fuel and open a safe working lane.
- **Later effect:** a sound crossing leaves the repaired soil route biologically active and heat-ready instead of scorched.

### Restored corridor

The second segment travels beside or through whatever repair the party built for the soilbearers. The correct method depends on that repair. Canvas troughs need wet backing. Copper scent-rills conduct heat and must be isolated from dry packing. Hand-ferry routes require crews to clear before ignition. A shaded detour may need a carried ember rather than the original front.

- **Primary problem:** deliver heat after living soil has passed, not through the beetle stream.
- **Useful boundaries:** old-ground ribbons, wet capillary lines, lifted bridge pieces, and already-charred scar tissue.
- **Common choice:** pause soil delivery briefly, split labor between animal control and fire control, or risk overlap to preserve time.
- **Later effect:** a working corridor can carry both soil and bounded heat in sequence, creating several heat-ready shells.

### Crownward seam

The final segment approaches a root gap that opens only on the Bearer's deep exhale. Lantern pollen may already cross above it, and the selected fungal course may pass nearby in wet cords.

- **Primary problem:** synchronize the front with root-breath while protecting light, rain, and memory paths.
- **Useful boundaries:** cooled root lips, wet pollen stems, cleared crownward runners, and an ember held below the seam.
- **Common choice:** delay the main front, carry a small prepared ember, or accept a weak late heat current rather than risk an early jump.
- **Later effect:** prepared coats open during the safe interval instead of charring or remaining sealed.

## Preparing a bounded corridor

A defensible corridor has four elements.

- **Continuous intended fuel:** living blackgrass or a short prepared ember path that reaches the next living band.
- **Two independent margins:** wet, mineral, living-soil, or already-charred boundaries on both sides.
- **A prepared receiver:** renewed scar or filled shell path, not merely somewhere the party wants fire to go.
- **A maintained escape:** at least one route that does not cross the projected front or close on the same root pulse.

Available methods include:

### Clear lateral fuel

Move canvas, chaff, bedding, spice dust, cut stems, rope fibers, and loose wood away from both margins.

- **Requirements:** labor, time, and authority over salvage that may be damaged or abandoned.
- **Visible result:** the grass front remains low instead of throwing sparks into adjacent material.
- **Persistent cost:** useful cargo may be scattered, soaked, dismantled, or left behind.
- **Later option:** one margin can survive without continuous watering.

### Lay a returned wet line

Divert working basin water along a margin and return the unused flow through a lower gutter.

- **Requirements:** an intact source, path, and return; a watcher at the downstream receiver.
- **Visible result:** steam rises in a narrow line while root tissue behind it remains cool and flexible.
A dead-end splash looks equivalent for a few breaths but steams dry; only a line with an intact return stays cool through the passing front.
- **Persistent cost:** the water branch is committed during the burn and cannot simultaneously support a large caravan diversion.
- **Later option:** the corridor can pass near fungal cords or lantern stems without automatically destroying them.

### Build a living-soil guide

Use delivered old ground as a dark, moist ribbon at the edge of the intended front. Blackgrass bends toward the renewal scar and stops at healthy pellets.

- **Requirements:** working soil delivery and protection from oil, sterile salt, and crushing traffic.
- **Visible result:** heat crosses above the guide while beetle pellets remain dark and biologically active.
- **Persistent cost:** the soil route cannot carry heavy human loads during the crossing.
- **Later option:** the same corridor can deliver soil first and heat second to several crown shells.

### Make a mineral break

Clear down to nonflammable shell, stone, wet clay, or clean metal fittings. White Salt alone is not a safe break near the Glass Waste; reflective crystals can intensify heat.

- **Requirements:** tools and a route for removed hot material.
- **Visible result:** the flame shortens and turns inward at the cleared strip.
- **Persistent cost:** the break may sever shallow rootlets or close a soilbearer shortcut.
- **Later option:** a small crew can hold a threatened cargo edge without basin water.

### Hold and ferry an ember

Separate a small burning clump in a lidded shovel, wet clay cradle, stone tray, or clean iron basket, then carry it across a temporarily closed gap to prepared living blackgrass.

- **Requirements:** a receiving band, heat protection, and a route cleared of pollen and dry dust.
- **Visible result:** the main front can be delayed while the later segment remains possible.
- **Persistent cost:** the carried ember weakens quickly and becomes dangerous if fed cut grass or oil.
- **Later option:** the party can wait for root-breath rather than forcing the entire front against a closed seam.

### Delay one segment

Strip a short section of blackgrass with roots intact, cool it below ignition, or lift it away from friction until the receiver is ready.

- **Requirements:** careful handling and a plan to reconnect the heat path.
- **Visible result:** the front stops at a clean gap instead of scattering.
- **Persistent cost:** delay consumes Root Night access and may produce a weak late current.
- **Later option:** soil, light, rain, or memory can arrive before heat.

## Running the burn

Use this sequence once ignition is chosen.

1. **Name the segment and receiver.** “Protect the wagons” is not enough; state where the front should end.
2. **Show both margins.** Identify the people, water, material, or living system holding each one.
3. **Move nonparticipants and animals.** A controlled operation still needs a fallback route.
4. **Ignite or admit the front.** Use existing blackgrass whenever possible. Added accelerant creates an uncontrolled fuel path.
5. **Check source, margins, receiver, and neighbor.** Show what burned, what stayed cool, whether the intended receiver changed, and what adjacent current was strained.
6. **Record the scar.** A successful segment leaves a visible line of blackened sheath with flexible damp tissue and living soil behind it.

Let failure follow the method: a wet line runs dry, a mineral break reflects heat, an animal crosses a margin, an ember fades before the seam opens, or oil starts a second front. Never substitute a generic loss of control for a consequence already present in the fiction.

## Current and hazard states

Record **bounded blackgrass heat** separately from any **runaway fire**.

- **Absent heat current:** the intended corridor is fully smothered, severed, diverted away from prepared receivers, or missed after the crown hardens.
- **Weak heat current:** intermittent or late heat reaches part of the prepared path; one filled shell may open, or the corridor may require a costly second ember.
- **Working heat current:** a low continuous front reaches the prepared renewal scar and crownward receiver after the other currents arrive.
- **Strong heat current:** both margins are redundant, a held ember or second living branch exists, and the working front can absorb one later gap, dry patch, or shortened breath interval.

A runaway fire is not a strong current. Track it as a separate front with its own fuel, margins, and threatened receivers. Crews may abandon the intended heat current to contain it, split their work, or accept damage in one region to preserve another.

## People and property in the burn

**Pelen Marr** knows the wagon fittings and accepts responsibility for the crushed road. Pelen will dismantle damaged company wood and personal shares with consent, but will not claim that guilt gives him title to everyone else's cargo.

**Mara Doss**, **Oren Pike**, and the teamsters can move animals before ignition or use trained teams to drag wet lines and heavy breaks. Animals left near whitening grass become a route problem before they become casualties.

**Ira Senn** owns the longest intact copper. Ira may lend it for a returned wet line if the pipe remains recoverable or if the party states why losing it is necessary. Heating sealed or oil-tainted copper can burst it.

**Corven Ash** owns the spice load whose dust can carry flame. Corven will sacrifice contaminated bags once shown the front. They resist destroying sealed stock merely because spice is present somewhere nearby.

**Nahl Reed** insists that burning the only viable seed is not justified by calling fire natural. Nahl can recognize a prepared shell but cannot command the operation.

## Complications and failure-forward consequences

- Oil ignites along a shallow seam. Isolate the second front, abandon nearby salvage, or divert the main heat current away from the road.
- A wet margin protects the fungal braid but drains faster than expected. The course survives while the heat current becomes weak, or vice versa.
- Lantern pollen arrives above the corridor before the crew clears cut stems. Close one light path, delay ignition, or risk a crownward jump.
- A draft animal crosses a cleared break. Recovering it may scatter fuel, consume the escape route, or require the teamsters to abandon another operation.
- A successful wagon-scar crossing reaches a closed crown seam. An ember hold, delayed segment, or the Bearer's preliminary breath is needed to test the gap.
- The front is fully smothered to save people. The adventure continues with an absent heat current: prepared knots remain sealed unless the party can establish a later ember route.

Preserving life may close the seed route. Record the changed state without grading the choice.

## Stage changes

- **Long Shade:** the distant smoke and old scar can be studied; fuel can be moved before the front arrives.
- **Red Dusk:** the fire crosses the wagon scar and restored road. Heavy breaks and salvage decisions must already be in place.
- **Root Night:** a bounded front or held ember can pass the crownward seam on the deep exhale.
- **Glass Dawn:** reflected light creates a second ignition risk. A late operation becomes containment and departure rather than careful preparation.

## Results and later options

After the burn, record:

- the state of each segment: wagon scar, restored corridor, and crownward seam;
- the source and both margins used;
- exceptional fuel removed, spent, or left in place;
- whether the soil route remained biologically active;
- whether lantern, rain, or memory paths were strained;
- whether a runaway front exists and what it threatens;
- whether the bounded heat current is absent, weak, working, or strong;
- whether an ember remains available for the deep breath; and
- which people, animals, cargo, and exits remain on each side of the scar.

Leave the scar with an exact account of what the fire opened, what it consumed, and what it still threatens.

## Late access and moving evidence

The fire front is itself a moving carrier. Opened shells, whitening margins, smoke behavior, and a held ember can preserve burn evidence after the party leaves the old scar. Record the clue under the Blackgrass Burn and keep the intended front separate from any runaway fire.

Avoiding the burn may knowingly leave the crown coat sealed. A late crew may ferry a held ember only along a crownward seam already prepared with fuel continuity, two margins, a receiver, and an escape route. Once Glass Dawn reflection creates an uncontrolled second ignition, excess flame cannot be relabeled as bounded heat, and a missed crownward seam cannot be improvised after the coat hardens.

encounters.title: Root-Breath Chamber
encounters.summary: Inside the Bearer's load chamber, crews read burden, cooling, and rhythm to favor one route band and prepare for a single nonrepeatable deep exhale.
encounters.opening_view: A wagon bell stops midway through a swing. Dust, hair, and canvas lift as the ground rises and holds. Warm mist pours from a seam wide enough to show iron trapped in old root, one dry cooling channel, and bands straining out of time. Then the outer leaves turn their pale undersides east. The chamber has stopped pulling. Somewhere above, the crown begins to descend.
encounters.content:
## Situation

The Bearer moves without legs. Long bands tighten in sequence, lift portions of the root mat, and draw the forest east. Warm rain cools the working tissue. Vents shed heat. Old ground, fungal cords, lantern stems, and crown channels all cross the same bodily rhythm.

During Root Night, the central mound opens between the load roots. Here weight, cooling, traction, and obstruction become visible; no brain, shrine, mouth, or court waits behind them. Embedded iron holds one band too long. A dry return channel overheats another. Uneven caravan loads pull the western mat out of rhythm.

Small corrections can open a gate, ease a route, or make the coming breath more readable. They cannot make the Bearer understand an appeal. One preliminary breath tests the system. One long central exhale slackens the mature crown sockets. Then the inward draw hardens them. The sequence does not repeat for regret.

## The Bearer's cycle

Use four observable phases. Characters can learn them in several regions before entering the chamber.

| Phase | Physical signs | What opens or closes | Safe work |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Traction pulse | Outer root bands tighten in sequence; loose lines draw taut; dust moves east | Broad outer paths shift; crown stems remain under load | Move with the pulse, measure sequence, redistribute light burdens |
| Venting rise | Chamber air warms; small vents open west to east; basin water descends into cooling channels | Root gates and service seams open briefly | Clear vents, cool tissue, test a gate, induce a small preliminary exhale |
| Long central exhale | Traction stops; suspended lines slacken; crown stems soften; the chamber floor settles | Crownward seam, seed sockets, and selected inner routes open together | Transfer heat, complete convergence, realign one load band, separate a mature seed during the later slack interval |
| Inward draw and hardening | Air reverses, wet cords tighten, crown fibers draw firm, eastern tissue takes a glassy sheen | Service paths narrow; cut tissue tears; outer routes close faster | Clear the chamber, commit to departure or continued migration, accept work not completed |

The safe separation interval occurs after the exhale has opened the crown and before the inward draw tightens the wet cords. It should be announced by several signs, not hidden behind a secret count.

## Reading the cycle

Three independent indicators establish a reliable timing model.

- **Suspended tension:** tie or observe lines across separate roots. They loosen only during the long exhale.
- **Vent sequence:** warm vents open west to east, pause below the central mound, then release one cooler sustained flow.
- **Water temperature:** a marked basin branch cools the inner tissue during venting, becomes nearly still during the exhale, and is drawn sharply inward afterward.
- **Cord behavior:** fungal lines brighten and relax at Root Night, then tighten enough to cut soft material during the inward draw.
- **Fire seam:** the crownward blackgrass gap opens only when the deeper exhale separates its root lips.

Two indicators identify a likely phase. Three establish a defensible working interval. A strong pulse current has an additional redundant cue or a corrected burden that lengthens the slack period.

Once these signs are established, state the current phase. Use a system check for finishing rigging, holding position under load, or preserving a route while several indicators are watched.

## Burden map

The Bearer incorporates obstacles rather than instantly expelling them. Stone tools, shell ornaments, animal bone, wagon iron, and corroded metal from earlier crossings lie at different depths. Some are harmless scars. Others divert pressure into neighboring roots.

At the opening of the chamber, identify four burden classes.

| Burden | Sign | Safe response | Dangerous mistake |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Exposed foreign object | Metal or stone protrudes from flexible tissue; warmth and discoloration radiate around it | Support the load, remove it along the entry path, cool the pocket | Lever sideways against a live root or assume every embedded object is harmful |
| Incorporated scar | New tissue has grown evenly around an old object; pulse passes symmetrically | Leave it, record it, remove only loose surface material | Treat the chamber as a treasure vault and cut structural tissue |
| Active pressure bridge | One object or wagon load transfers force between two tightening bands | Redistribute weight before removal; brace both sides | Pull the bridge during traction and trigger a collapse or route jump |
| Blocked channel | Heat rises behind metal, silt, crushed wood, or pinched root sheath | Open the existing water or vent path; remove the obstruction in pieces | Flood blindly, seal the vent, or cut a new channel through load tissue |

Diagnosis matters more than extraction. An old royal ornament may be harmless while a plain wagon tire compresses a live cooling channel.

## Correcting burdens

### Remove exposed iron

Support the surrounding root, reproduce the object's entry angle, cool the pocket, and draw the iron out during venting rather than traction.

- **Visible result:** local heat falls and the next pulse passes with less guarding tension.
- **Persistent cost:** the iron may bend, the support rig may be trapped, or the removal may consume the only heavy lever available elsewhere.
- **Later option:** the deep exhale becomes longer or more symmetrical, and one crown channel may open that was previously pinched.

### Redistribute carried weight

Move wagons, cargo, people, and draft teams from one load root to another before the central exhale.

- **Visible result:** one root band lifts while another settles; outer regions change relative position.
- **Persistent cost:** a favored route gains access while an unfavored route narrows sooner.
- **Later option:** A stranded group may settle nearer an exit, a central ecology route may stay open, or crown access may lower.

### Restore cooling

Open an existing basin channel, remove a pinch, or route a temporary returned flow through a hot burden pocket.

- **Visible result:** vent air cools, pulse intervals lengthen, and root tissue changes from hard dry tension to flexible contraction.
- **Persistent cost:** the water branch is committed during Root Night and may no longer support another diversion.
- **Later option:** a weak breath can become working, or a working breath can absorb one later strain.

### Release dead sheath

Cut or peel only tissue that is dry, separated, and no longer carrying pulse. Living load roots darken, warm, and tighten under pressure; dead sheath remains cool and flakes away.

- **Visible result:** a vent, service seam, or old removal path reopens without changing the traction sequence.
- **Persistent cost:** the route may become rough, exposed, or one-way.
- **Later option:** a burden can be removed or a crew can escape without cutting live structure.

### Match the migration rhythm

Repeated vibration through ropes, wagon spokes, drums, footfalls, or tools can reinforce the venting sequence when it matches the Bearer's existing rhythm.

- **Visible result:** small gates open in order and a brief preliminary exhale follows.
- **Persistent cost:** mismatched force creates guarding tension, shortens the next interval, or shifts a nearby region unexpectedly.
- **Later option:** Routes and timing can be tested before the unique deep exhale.

The beat accommodates physiology. It neither speaks for the Bearer nor wins agreement.

## Preliminary breath

A preliminary breath is a smaller venting response induced before the long central exhale. It can:

- open one service gate;
- slacken a trapped wagon line;
- test the blackgrass crownward seam;
- expose a hidden burden pocket;
- shift one outer region by a short distance; or
- confirm the sequence of cues.

It cannot safely release a mature seed. Crown sockets remain under longitudinal tension even when nearby lines loosen.

Inducing more than one substantial preliminary breath without correcting the underlying burden strains the system. The next deep exhale becomes shorter, hotter, or asymmetric. A careful test creates information; repeated forcing spends the final window.

## Limited redirection

Moving weight, cooling one side, freeing an obstruction, or matching the local pulse can favor one of three broad load bands. The Bearer continues east. Redirection changes which regions draw together during the next phase; it does not turn the forest around.

| Favored band | Immediate movement | Opportunity created | Opportunity strained |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Western carry band | Camp and the forked-wagon roots settle closer to the last ordinary ground | Easier mass departure, late rescue, or animal extraction | Crown and burn seam rise farther from the western camp route |
| Middle circulation band | Basins, voice hollow, and chamber remain mutually reachable through Root Night | Stronger water, memory, and cooling transfer; better split-party return | Outer exits narrow earlier and heavy wagons become harder to recover intact |
| Crownward lift band | The rain crown and crownward fire seam descend toward the chamber | Easier convergence, heat transfer, and seed work | Camp loses direct crown access and undecided travelers need an immediate departure plan |

A strong correction may preserve one neighboring band as well. A weak or improvised redirection creates the intended opportunity but closes the strained route earlier. State the trade before the final shift whenever the characters have enough evidence to perceive it.

## The deep exhale

The long central exhale occurs once during Root Night. Forcing the Bearer under unresolved strain brings it early; preserved cooling lets the natural sequence complete later.

Run it as a visible operation.

1. **Call the venting rise.** Warm air opens west to east. Crews take positions and clear routes.
2. **Show traction stopping.** Root bands cease drawing east. Suspended lines remain taut for one moment.
3. **Open the exhale.** Air and moisture move outward, gates separate, and prepared fire can cross the crownward seam.
4. **Announce crown slack.** Ropes, fungal cords, and seed stems visibly loosen. This is the safe working interval.
5. **Show the first inward cue.** Loose water reverses, pale cords begin to tighten, or eastern bark takes a reflective sheen.
6. **Close the interval.** Any crew still cutting or crossing must release, retreat, accept damage, or continue east with the forest.

The exact number of actions depends on the game system and prior preparation. The important fact is that the interval is readable and finite. A strong root pulse may allow one correction after a complication; a weak pulse may complete only one prepared operation cleanly.

## Root-pulse current states

Before the cycle is understood, mark the pulse **unassessed**, not absent.

- **Absent:** the deep exhale has passed, the crown connection is severed, or sealed vents and catastrophic burden prevent a usable slack interval.
- **Weak:** the exhale is shortened, asymmetric, overheated, or dependent on an unresolved pressure bridge. One major operation can complete cleanly; another incurs strain or damage.
- **Working:** venting, cooling, crown slack, and inward cues occur in a readable sequence long enough for prepared transfers and one safe separation.
- **Strong:** burdens are balanced, cooling is working, vents are open, and at least three independent cues confirm a longer or redundant interval. The pulse can absorb one late rigging fault, strained neighboring current, or route correction.

A strong pulse does not create a seed. It makes the final convergence and separation physically possible under greater strain.

## People in the chamber

**Pelen Marr** recognizes old wagon iron by shape and stress. Shame makes him eager to strip every foreign fitting from the chamber. Require him to distinguish a harmful burden from material the Bearer has carried safely for decades.

**Nahl Reed** watches temperature, return flow, and crown tension. They can say whether a correction improves the six paths. They cannot translate improvement into desire.

**The route recorder** keeps reports moving. A shifted band is useful only when the people depending on it hear the new capacity and the sign that will close it.

**Mara Doss**, or another teamster, can use recovered animals to redistribute weight. The animals feel the venting rise early, but bringing them inside spends calm, footing, and handler attention.

**Jun Alder** sees that the forest is capable of carrying people east. Capability is not safety, destiny, or consent. The chamber supplies a road, not a command.

## Hazards and failure-forward consequences

- An object proves to be an active pressure bridge. Brace it, leave it, or accept a route shift rather than pulling it free.
- A cooling repair drains a basin branch needed elsewhere. The breath improves while rain or fire control becomes weak.
- A rhythm test opens the wrong service gate. A stranded group gains a route, but the intended crown path narrows.
- A cut reaches living tissue. The Bearer guards the wound, shortening the exhale and moving pressure into a neighboring band.
- A heavy load is moved too late. It still favors the chosen route, but someone or something cannot return across the settling root.
- The safe interval is missed. A mature seed remains attached, can be torn free with explicit damage, or can be followed east for another uncertain opportunity. Do not retroactively invent a second clean breath.
- The chamber partially collapses after a burden is removed. Use dead-sheath routes, braces, or continued eastward movement; do not end play simply because the original entrance closes.

Failure changes the available geometry and the quality of the pulse. It does not make the Bearer vindictive.

## Stage changes

- **Long Shade:** the chamber is sealed, but root pulses, vents, and burden responses can be observed elsewhere.
- **Red Dusk:** warm vents become obvious and preliminary-breath tests become possible from service seams.
- **Root Night:** the chamber opens, one load band can be favored, and the unique deep exhale occurs.
- **Glass Dawn:** the chamber closes behind the inward draw. Eastern tissue hardens and anyone inside must exit west immediately or continue with the forest.

## Results and later options

Before leaving the chamber, record:

- the three or more cues used to read the cycle;
- exposed objects removed, incorporated scars left intact, pressure bridges supported, and channels restored;
- the state of cooling and any basin branch committed;
- preliminary breaths induced and the strain they caused;
- which load band was favored and which route narrowed;
- whether the root-pulse current is absent, weak, working, or strong;
- the announced sign that begins safe crown slack;
- the announced sign that ends it; and
- which crews, departure groups, and ecological transfers are positioned for the deep exhale.

The chamber provides timing, access, and limited leverage over a living body. Physiology grants no permission.

## Late access and external evidence

The Bearer's cycle can be read outside the chamber through wagon ropes, basin returns, blackgrass bowing, opening vents, crown-stem tension, feeder slack, and the Glass Verge's hardening interval. A late crew may still time the deep exhale with at least three independent cues and a prepared cradle and feeder ring.

Late access does not restore a missed preliminary-breath test, a complete burden map, broad redirection, or lost cooling time. Allow at most the corrections physically supported by prior observation and staged materials. After the inward draw the chamber closes. The Bearer does not provide a second clean-separation exhale.

encounters.title: Crown of Unfallen Rain
encounters.summary: The descending crown exposes every missing relationship and distinguishes empty shell, stormglass, viable seed, mature knot, and demonstrated surplus.
encounters.opening_view: The crown comes down roots-first, carrying weather in clear knots. Soil enters one stem and the inner membrane darkens. Gold follows another; water finds a third and returns as mist. At the center, a hard-coated knot turns a small cloud around an empty place. It is close enough now to touch. The six feeder paths are not all answering.
encounters.content:
## Situation

The Crown of Unfallen Rain is a descending lattice, not a fruit tree. Six paths enter its wet translucent stems: old soil, captured dawn, circulating rain, remembered river course, bounded blackgrass heat, and the Bearer's pulse. Where all six coincide, a clear knot closes around a turning cloud.

Every earlier choice is visible here. Delivered ground darkens several stems. Living pollen writes gold through wet tissue. Returning water fogs a knot and clears again. A selected fungal braid gives the cloud a stable course. Bounded heat opens the coat. A balanced pulse lifts the feeder ring.

Keep the crown an honest receiver. It displays what was repaired, spent, or damaged; absent paths stay absent.

## Reading an unfinished knot

A careful look identifies a missing current without a roll. Uncertainty may concern how quickly the defect can be corrected, how much material the correction requires, or whether the next physical signal will arrive first.

| Missing or failed current | Visible defect |
| --- | --- |
| Living old soil | The knot is clear through the center; no dark motes root into the inner membrane |
| Captured dawn | Water gathers, but the cloud fades after one release and does not renew its own light |
| Circulating rain | Moisture enters and does not return; a white salt rind forms along the lower seam |
| Remembered river course | Condensation wanders, pools against the wrong wall, or spills without a stable fall and overflow relation |
| Bounded blackgrass heat | The outer coat remains sealed and waxy, even when the inner weather turns correctly |
| Bearer root pulse | The knot fills but never beats; its feeder stems stay load-bearing instead of becoming a separable socket |

A damaged current may produce a mixed sign. For example, fouled rain can leave both an oily return and a salt rind. State each observed defect separately; do not collapse the crown into a single quality score.

## Knot states

Use these states for each examined knot.

| State | Requirements | What it can do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Empty shell | At least one current absent | Holds evidence of the missing relationship but cannot sustain weather |
| Stormglass knot | All six currents have touched it, but one remains weak, interrupted, or incorrectly related | Produces brief local weather and preserves useful structure; it is not a self-establishing watershed |
| Viable knot | All six currents work at the receiver through one complete crown circuit | Maintains a small internal cloud, returns its water, and follows the selected course |
| Mature knot | Viable; its coat has opened under bounded heat; its internal pulse continues after the feeders slacken | Can be cleanly separated during the deep exhale |
| Surplus crown | At least two mature knots are visible while living-soil delivery continues | One mature knot can be removed without taking the only demonstrated continuation of the migration |

A strong current can absorb one concrete strain that would otherwise make an adjacent current weak during the circuit. It cannot make an absent current present, supply a missing river relation, or turn a sealed coat into a mature seed.

## The crown sequence

The six currents are relationships, not objects placed into sockets. Run the following sequence, with prepared groups acting in parallel.

### 1. Descend and diagnose

The crown comes within reach during Root Night. Show two or more knots with different defects. More knots may be inspected, but eastern stems harden first and each heavy intervention competes with departure work.

A diagnosis should answer:

- which currents reach this knot now;
- which path each current uses;
- which receiver sign is present or absent;
- whether a weak state is local to the knot or inherited from the source; and
- which physical change will announce the next closure.

### 2. Choose a receiver

Choose which knot receives scarce labor and material: concentrate on one defensible seed, preserve several candidates until the strongest declares itself, or repair their common path.

Changing receiver after heat has opened a coat sacrifices that prepared shell. Changing before heat costs route and time but does not automatically destroy either knot.

### 3. Complete the living paths

Each current must reach the selected knot through a functioning path.

- **Soil:** living old ground arrives as dark mist from a road still used by soilbearers or through an equivalent uncontaminated living route.
- **Dawn:** glasswings or wet pollen carry stored light from an intact lantern release; ordinary reflection does not substitute.
- **Rain:** water passes through the knot and returns to a basin branch rather than ending in the shell.
- **Course:** a living fungal braid impresses fall, storage, ground, and overflow relations compatible with Merewash; a transcription can guide the work but cannot supply the living path.
- **Heat:** the crownward seam receives a low bounded front only after the other four material relationships are present.
- **Pulse:** a crownward channel carries the Bearer's beat through the knot before the long central exhale.

When a path is completed, show both the knot's response and one response at the source or return. A rain circuit is not working merely because the knot becomes wet.

### 4. Close one crown circuit

A viable knot must pass one complete circuit before the deep exhale:

1. dark motes root into the inner membrane;
2. stored dawn brightens the cloud from within;
3. rain enters, crosses the cloud, and returns;
4. condensation follows the selected fall and overflow relation;
5. bounded heat opens a narrow germination seam; and
6. the knot continues its own small pulse between two Bearer beats.

If one sign fails, the unclosed current is visible and may be corrected while the next warning develops. Do not demand six separate random successes after the relationships have already been established elsewhere.

## Separating a seed

A mature rain-seed is basket-sized, heavy with moving water, and awkward rather than enormous. Two people can carry it in a wet flexible cradle; one calm draft animal can bear it as a balanced load. A sealed chest, dry sack, or rigid clamp interrupts its circulation.

### Clean physical separation

All five conditions are required:

1. the selected knot is mature;
2. its water has completed a return after the coat opened;
3. a wet cradle or equivalent support already bears its weight;
4. at least three independent deep-exhale cues have appeared; and
5. the party draws the slack feeder ring free before the inward draw hardens it.

The feeder ring opens like a soft socket during the deep exhale. A blade is unnecessary when the conditions are met. The empty socket closes without bleeding sap, the remaining crown keeps its pulse, and the separated seed continues cycling in the cradle.

### Ecologically defensible separation

A clean separation is a demonstrated surplus only when all of the following are also true:

- living-soil delivery remains at least working after the selected knot matures;
- at least one other mature knot remains attached and continues its own circuit; and
- no runaway fire or severed common return is consuming the crown's remaining redundancy.

This establishes visible continuation east. It grants no consent and leaves the Glass Waste uncertain.

### Other separations

| Method or state | Immediate result | Continuing consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mature knot, clean exhale, no surplus | The seed remains viable and the socket closes cleanly | The only demonstrated mature continuation has been taken; crown and basin behavior deteriorate eastward |
| Stormglass knot during the exhale | The partial knot comes free without tearing the crown | It can produce bounded local weather but requires repair before it can establish a watershed |
| Any knot before the deep exhale | Feeders tear under load | One linked current falls a state, the crown is injured, and the carried knot inherits a torn relation |
| Any knot after the inward draw | Hardened tissue must be cut or broken | The seed is damaged, the route closes around the workers, and the eastern crown retains a permanent scar |
| Mature knot left attached | The forest carries the completed convergence east | Merewash receives measurements, methods, and any copied course, but no rain-seed |

## Failure-forward consequences

A failed crown operation should change a named relationship before it destroys the whole finale.

- A feeder slips: the knot falls from viable to stormglass, but remains supportable in its cradle.
- Heat arrives early: one shell dies while another candidate remains unburned.
- The living braid separates: the course survives in transcription, but the knot no longer has a living memory path.
- The return branch tears: the seed can be carried wet, but circulation must be rebuilt before planting.
- The deep exhale is missed: leave the seed, travel east toward another physiological opportunity not guaranteed by the old account, or damage crown and seed by forcing separation.
- The cradle fails after clean release: carriers can save the seed by abandoning another hand load, route position, or animal task.

Name the lost route, state, burden, or redundancy immediately. Do not convert one weak operation into an unexplained total ecological collapse.

## What the crown cannot decide

The crown can show an empty shell, sealed coat, torn feeder, complete return, mature knot, and surplus. It cannot weigh Merewash against the forest, assign ownership, spend another person's cargo, or choose Jun's road. Matter narrows a claim without becoming a judge.

## Late access and receiver diagnosis

An unfinished knot can diagnose a missing or malformed current even when the source region is no longer reachable. The defect identifies the failed relation; it does not recreate source material, reopen a closed path, or award every unobserved clue from the earlier region. A correction is possible only through a living path, carried current, or prepared bypass that still physically reaches the chosen knot.

After the deep exhale, clean separation is no longer available. Crews may leave the knots attached, accept a stormglass or sealed state, tear a knot free with the stated injury, carry a knot detached earlier, or continue east. Do not extend the physiological window because the procedure was understood late.

encounters.title: Glass Verge
encounters.summary: Reflected dawn reduces three departure routes while rescue, seed separation, and individual decisions proceed in parallel across the last White Salt.
encounters.opening_view: The first wagon reaches the salt shelf as dawn kindles beneath the leaves. Its axle grinds; behind it, a litter team waits for room, and above them the crown service root hangs slack for one breath. Eastward, the forest is already taking back the ground. Hessa reads the roster over wheels, bells, and rising heat. Each name answers west, east, or not yet.
encounters.content:
## Situation

The Glass Verge is the moving edge between the western roots and the last White Salt a person can still reach on foot. Dawn appears first as reflection. Eastern tissue hardens. The crown follows from east to west. Broad routes lose capacity before they vanish.

By Root Night the caravan may be whole, divided, or still searching. The crown may hold no viable knot, one knot the forest needs, or a demonstrated surplus. Chamber work may have favored the western carry band, wet middle band, or crownward service root. Display accumulated state rather than presenting a menu; the finale adds no preset solutions.

At the verge every report becomes a body, load, animal, cradle, injury, or unresolved name. Keep distinct people from disappearing inside “the caravan.”

## The three departure routes

These are route families, not guaranteed corridors. Earlier rescue, burden correction, basin work, and Bearer redirection determine their exact starting points and how long they remain usable.

| Route | Capacity while open | Principal limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Broad salt shelf | Walkers, assisted people, litters, calm teams, dismantled wagons, and at first an intact light wagon | Farthest from the crown; it loses wagon capacity at the inward draw and all contact at direct sun |
| Wet middle ledge | Walkers, assisted people, single-file animals, hand loads, and one carried person at a time | Requires a working cooled basin edge; no intact wagon and no panicked team |
| Crown service root | Crown workers, climbers, one supported litter or rain-seed cradle, and compact tools | Opens fully only on the deep exhale and closes at the inward draw; it cannot carry wagons or loose animals |

A favored western carry band extends the broad shelf through one additional heavy movement. A favored middle circulation band keeps the wet ledge cool and broad enough for an additional carried person or animal passage. A favored crownward lift band brings the service root closer to the crown and lets a prepared seed team reach it without another transfer. Each effect changes a route’s capacity or duration.

If a route was damaged or never established, state the reduced capacity. Do not quietly restore it because the finale has begun.

## The dawn signals

Use four visible signals rather than a hidden round count.

### First reflection

The easternmost crown stems turn mirror-bright, blackgrass smolders without contact, and the broad shelf begins shedding salt. At this signal, intact wagons, most animals, and people not remaining for crown work should already be moving.

Show it before heavy departure closes. A prepared group already moving can finish its crossing. Beginning a new heavy salvage operation now means knowingly surrendering an earlier exit.

### Deep exhale

At least three cues coincide: root lines slacken, vent leaves turn outward, basin surfaces flatten, pale cords lose tension, the crown drops a handspan, or blackgrass flame leans inward. The crown service root opens, mature sockets soften, and clean seed separation becomes possible.

The exhale is also the last reliable interval for a supported litter from crown or chamber to reach the service root. It is not long enough to improvise every missing preparation from nothing.

### Inward draw

Water draws east, the vents close, crown stems harden, and the service root contracts. The broad shelf no longer accepts an intact wagon. The wet ledge remains only where circulation and cooling were preserved. Anyone still at the crown must leave by a prepared line, accept a damaging forced route, or continue east.

### Direct sun

The first direct sun touches the Glass Waste. Reflected heat produces a second fire threat, the last roots lift from salt, and ordinary westward footing ends. A crown knot that missed its living dawn filament remains dark in the glare; reflection does not backfill the broken path. People still aboard enter a hotter, faster migration with reduced supplies, no familiar exit, and no assurance of another clean separation interval.

## Departure muster

Run departure planning as an operational record, not a vote that binds everyone.

1. **Count:** Hessa or another recorder names everyone physically seen, everyone unresolved, and everyone whose location is known only by report.
2. **State capacities:** route leaders state which people, animals, litters, wagons, and loads each open route can actually carry.
3. **Give the current plan:** each departure group hears where it is going, what physical signal closes its route, and whether the seed attempt changes its timing.
4. **Record choice:** mark first-departure, rescue remainder, seed group, unresolved, physically unable, or voluntary eastbound status separately.
5. **Assign support:** name carriers, handlers, guides, route keepers, and who takes responsibility when a principal worker leaves.
6. **Send a record:** each westbound group carries the names and intentions known when it departed; later groups do not become unaccounted merely because they chose a different time.

A person may leave without approving seed-taking. A person may help complete the seed and still leave west. A person may continue east only after immediate rescue or stabilization has made that a real choice. Silence, absence, injury, youth, dependency, and admiration are not consent.

## Running the finale in parallel

The crown and verge should normally be active at the same time.

When a seed clears the service root, show it beside any attached mature knot and name whether soilbearers still enter the crown. Only that simultaneous view establishes whether one cloud leaves while another travels east.

- At first reflection, Orra or another route leader sends the heavy first departure while the crown team diagnoses and prepares a receiver.
- Before the deep exhale, crown workers complete any final living path, settle who bears the seed, and place people who need the service root.
- During the deep exhale, the seed team may perform one clean separation while prepared departure teams use the service root and other open routes.
- At the inward draw, remaining westbound people take the last routes their bodies and burdens can use. Workers who stay name what they are staying to do.
- At direct sun, record everyone still aboard, their supplies, the forest states they can observe, and whether their continuing search or repair remains possible.

Split parties are expected. One group does not lose its action because another acts elsewhere. Advance the signal when the underlying physical event occurs, after showing its approach and resolving work already underway.

## Principal positions at the verge

These are starting judgments, not commands.

- **Orra Venn** sends a functioning caravan core west before the verge becomes heroic. She leaves with the last group whose route remains her responsibility unless she names and confirms a transfer.
- **Hessa Clay** reads every unresolved and eastbound name aloud. She will not let “the caravan left” conceal two people who did not.
- **Nahl Reed** supports carrying a demonstrated surplus. They oppose calling a sole, unopened, or unreturned knot harmless and count departure without a seed as a real success.
- **Pelen Marr** stays for the repair his wagon caused if his body permits. He offers his frame, labor, and judgment; he does not volunteer Ira's pipe or Corven's grain.
- **Sio Tern** remains until the selected course has been tested and copied. They will not let an inherited line certify a condition nobody observed.
- **Jun Alder** may travel east only after rescue, food, water, shelter, likely isolation, possible nonreturn, and an actual western route have all been named. Wonder is not a proxy for choice.

## Failure-forward departures

A failed crossing changes who or what can use the route next.

- A litter line parts: the person reaches safety, but two carriers and the replacement line end on opposite sides.
- An animal balks: its load can be divided, abandoned, or carried while the handler chooses whether to remain.
- A wagon grounds: people and hand loads cross; intact property does not.
- The seed cradle shifts: the seed can be stabilized by spending a hand load, route keeper, or animal capacity.
- A route margin burns: the intended group crosses, but the route closes behind it.
- A late worker misses the westward line: continued migration, shelter in a cooled basin, or another eastbound route becomes the next problem instead of immediate offscreen death.

## Final record

End play by writing one exact sentence for each subject:

- every traveler: westbound, eastbound, unresolved, injured, or dead;
- each draft animal and the burden it carried;
- the condition of the three wagon pockets and any people still within them;
- each of the six ecological currents;
- bounded heat and any separate runaway fire;
- the Bearer's burden, favored band, and deep-exhale state;
- every mature, stormglass, torn, or attached crown knot;
- whether any separation was clean and whether it was a demonstrated surplus;
- the route and custodian of any carried seed;
- what Merewash actually receives besides or instead of a seed;
- the people who continue east and the supplies and obligations they carry; and
- property used, lost, disputed, ratified, or owed after dawn.

Several outcomes will be true together. Close when every name has a direction, every living relationship a state, and every surviving obligation a bearer.

## Late groups and closed westward access

The verge is a physical horizon and departure condition, not a clue-locked room. A group that reaches it late uses the capacity actually remaining on the broad shelf, wet ledge, or service root. Knowledge of an earlier route does not preserve its burden class, and a report not yet delivered cannot guide people who never heard it.

After direct sun, ordinary westward footing ends. Anyone still aboard continues east from the actual state of injuries, water, shelter, animals, fire, and current damage. Do not convert missed departure into automatic death or quietly reopen the salt behind the Bearer.

revelations.title: The missing wagons lie beyond the divided roots
revelations.description: Three bell notes, roster calls, animal traces, and the shape of the fork place five wagons and thirteen people in the separating root pockets.

revelations.title: The old ground travels by the Soilbearer Road
revelations.description: Dark pellets, empty westbound beetles, polished gates, and old-ground residue reveal the road carrying living earth toward the crown.

revelations.title: The Lantern Canopy carries borrowed dawn
revelations.description: Closed shining cups, glasswing moths, wet stems, and directed pollen mark the canopy where yesterday's light is lent forward.

revelations.title: Warm rain climbs through the western roots
revelations.description: Upward water, mineral warmth, climbing hoofprints, and capillary cords reveal the suspended basin chain.

revelations.title: The pale cords keep the measures of rivers
revelations.description: Repeated depths, slopes, intervals, and pale fungal lines lead to the hollow where earlier water observations still speak.

revelations.title: The blackgrass front is bearing down on the wagon scar
revelations.description: Smoke, whitening grass, heat-opened shells, and the old scar place the narrow burn before it reaches spilled caravan fuel.

revelations.title: The Bearer breathes beneath the central mound
revelations.description: Warm vents, shared root pulses, embedded burdens, and slackening crown stems reveal the load chamber that opens during Root Night.

revelations.title: Six paths descend into the rain crown
revelations.description: Old-ground mist, lantern pollen, warm rain, fungal braid, bounded heat, and root pulse converge in the descending lattice where clear knots form.

revelations.title: The Glass Verge is the last ground that will hold a walker
revelations.description: Reflected light, retreating salt, animal refusal, and the hardening root pulse mark the final western footing before dawn.

revelations.title: At dawn, the forest crosses onto glass
revelations.description: Reflected eastern light, western salt dust, root rhythm, warming bark, stored dawn, and the old account agree on direction and deadline.

revelations.title: The soilbearers carry old ground forward
revelations.description: Loaded beetles move living earth from western mounds into new receiver roots; empty beetles return for more instead of feeding on the forest.

revelations.title: Lantern flowers lend dawn; cut light goes nowhere
revelations.description: Stored light reaches the crown through living stem, moth, wet pollen, and receiver. A severed cup shines but leaves no filament.

revelations.title: The warm basins live by return
revelations.description: Marked water cools roots, wets fungal cords, opens lantern stems, reaches the crown, and comes back; draining the chain weakens every path it served.

revelations.title: The kept voices remember courses, not persons
revelations.description: Across repeated fragments, language, cadence, names, and kinship drift while slope, depth, mineral taste, distance, and interval remain.

revelations.title: Blackgrass must burn within living bounds
revelations.description: Old scars, opened shells, new roots, and crown defects show that low bounded heat renews the passage while an escaped front destroys it.

revelations.title: Only the deep exhale loosens a mature seed
revelations.description: The mature sockets slacken during the Bearer's one long central exhale and harden again with the inward draw; cuts outside that interval tear living channels.

revelations.title: A rain-seed is made where six paths meet
revelations.description: A mature knot requires living old soil, captured dawn, circulating rain, a remembered river course, blackgrass heat, and the Bearer's root pulse; no single tree bears it alone.

revelations.title: A repaired soil road can leave the forest a seed to spare
revelations.description: Restored living-soil delivery produces several maturing knots; without it, the visible convergence is enough only for the forest's own continuation.

clues.title: Three bells in one fork
clues.description: Three wagon bells answer from the same northeast divide: a high bronze note, a cracked iron note, and a muffled pair below both.
clues.discovery: separate the notes and mark their bearings

clues.title: Spice oil across the beetle detour
clues.description: Soilbearers turn around a stripe of spilled spice oil leading from the polished road toward the missing wagon pocket.

clues.title: The grain team's upward hoofprints
clues.description: Wet hoofprints climb from the lower root pocket toward the basin chain, proving at least one missing team came through the fork.

clues.title: Tovan's roster call in the cords
clues.description: A fresh fungal repetition carries Tovan Clay calling the missing names in order from below the divided roots.

clues.title: A wagon silhouette under reflected dawn
clues.description: From the verge, a suspended wagon and two separating root gullies are visible against the bright western salt.

clues.title: Dark earth on bronze backs
clues.description: Each eastbound beetle carries living soil unlike the dead White Salt; each empty beetle returns toward the western mounds.
clues.discovery: watch both streams long enough to see the return

clues.title: The polished track beneath the upper wheel
clues.description: The hanging wagon crushed a smooth, preexisting beetle road whose gates continue opening beyond the wreck.

clues.title: Pollen only on delivered ground
clues.description: Lantern pollen settles in bright lines where beetle-delivered soil darkens the roots, tracing the road below the canopy.

clues.title: Old-ground plugs in the inner gates
clues.description: The chamber contains compressed plugs of marsh, pine, shell, and river soil aligned with root channels from the west.

clues.title: A firebreak made of carried earth
clues.description: The blackgrass front stops at a dark ribbon built from beetle pellets, revealing the road by what does not burn.

clues.title: Dawn sealed above the camp
clues.description: The eastern sky remains dark while green-gold light shines through the seams of closed cups overhead.
clues.discovery: compare the sky with the canopy

clues.title: Glasswing scales in the soil mist
clues.description: Bright moth scales and pollen drift upward from the soil road toward a cluster of closed cups.

clues.title: Warm rain lighting the flower stems
clues.description: One basin circuit glows as it rises through translucent stems toward the closed lantern flowers.

clues.title: Dew climbing into warm roots
clues.description: Drops lift from low leaves, gather beneath a root, and join a warm cord running above the camp.
clues.discovery: follow one drop until it joins the flow

clues.title: Hoofprints filled from below
clues.description: The grain team's tracks fill with warm water rising through the soil, then climb toward a humid upper pocket.

clues.title: Capillary cords beneath the cups
clues.description: Translucent cords carry warm water past the lantern stems toward a higher chain of suspended pools.

clues.title: Voices sharpen when the cords wet
clues.description: A pulse of warm water makes the hollow's river measurements suddenly clear, and the pulse can be followed upward.

clues.title: Cooling channels in the chamber wall
clues.description: Warm channels enter the chamber from high westward roots and leave cooler toward the crown.

clues.title: A chain of steam above the western roots
clues.description: Reflected dawn reveals separate plumes rising in a stepped line toward the central canopy.

clues.title: One depth in changing voices
clues.description: A wet fungal line repeats the same well depth first in an old man's cadence and then in the voice of a child.
clues.discovery: wet the cord twice and compare what changes

clues.title: River clay threaded with speaking fungus
clues.description: One old-ground mound contains pale fungus that murmurs flood marks when warmed by a hand.

clues.title: Measurements traveling with the water
clues.description: Marked warm rain enters one cord and a sequence of remembered river distances sounds farther downslope.

clues.title: A voice-thread entering the incomplete knot
clues.description: One translucent knot pulses in time with a pale cord carrying repeated directions around a red stone.

clues.title: Silenced cords at the burn edge
clues.description: The fire has dried several pale strands; the surviving strands lead away from heat into a protected hollow.

clues.title: A low front crossing the forest
clues.description: The smoke remains a flat moving ribbon; it advances toward the wagon scar instead of rising from a fixed fire.
clues.discovery: track the smoke against a stationary branch

clues.title: Flowers opening ahead of heat
clues.description: Lantern cups begin opening in a line that advances from the east, marking the approaching warm front below.

clues.title: Heat pulse along the ancient scar
clues.description: The chamber wall warms in a narrow band aligned with an old blackened scar and the wagon break above.

clues.title: Five frames, one hidden body
clues.description: Wagons in separate pockets rise on the same deep pulse, followed by a warm breath through the roots beneath them.
clues.discovery: brace through two pulses and compare the timing

clues.title: Root gates opening on the exhale
clues.description: Crownward gates open in sequence only when the central mound releases warm air.

clues.title: Flame bowing away from the mound
clues.description: The blackgrass flame bends outward at regular intervals as a deep pressure wave leaves the center.

clues.title: Crown stems slackening together
clues.description: Every supporting stem loosens for a few breaths when the mound below expands.

clues.title: A breathing shadow beneath the canopy
clues.description: Reflected light shows the central forest rise and fall around one warm vent while outer roots tighten eastward.

clues.title: Pollen filaments converging inward
clues.description: The lantern release follows several bright threads toward one descending central lattice.

clues.title: Six traces in the crownward mist
clues.description: Old-ground minerals, gold pollen, fungal taste, char dust, root warmth, and basin water appear together in one mist feeding the lattice.
clues.discovery: mark the entering waters and sample the receiver mist

clues.title: River measures repeating above
clues.description: Selected course fragments travel upward through several cords and answer from a single high convergence.

clues.title: Pulse channels leading to the crown
clues.description: Six root channels leave the chamber in different materials and meet above the central-exhale seam.

clues.title: The last salt moving backward
clues.description: A stake set in ordinary salt falls behind the western roots at every traction pulse.
clues.discovery: set a fixed marker beyond the root mat

clues.title: Animals pulling toward the western light
clues.description: Freed draft animals consistently choose the broad root gully that ends on unglazed salt.

clues.title: Empty beetles turning before reflected heat
clues.description: Westbound soilbearers avoid one bright boundary and turn inland where the root mat still touches salt.

clues.title: Basins steaming toward the bright edge
clues.description: The lowest basins lose water rapidly near the reflective eastern boundary, marking the unsafe side of the forest.

clues.title: Second ignition in the glass reflection
clues.description: A patch of blackgrass ignites without contact where reflected dawn reaches the roots, identifying the coming glass line.

clues.title: The crown hardening from east to west
clues.description: Outer crown stems become glassy first on the bright side, showing which edge will become inaccessible.

clues.title: The sixth line meets the glass
clues.description: Sio's last line names loosening before the bright waste; the eastern reflection strengthens exactly as the western footing narrows.
clues.discovery: recite the line while watching both horizons

clues.title: Salt dust only on western bark
clues.description: Every exposed trunk carries salt dust on its western face, proving sustained eastward travel through the night.

clues.title: The empty return stream moving west
clues.description: Unladen soilbearers walk against the forest's motion while the entire road shifts east beneath them.

clues.title: Stored dawn releasing before true sunrise
clues.description: Lantern flowers begin their final release while the eastern reflection intensifies, linking the migration cycle to dawn.

clues.title: Basin temperature rising from the east
clues.description: Successive pools warm in east-to-west order as reflected light approaches the root mat.

clues.title: Earlier voices naming a glass crossing
clues.description: Several unrelated river fragments end with measurements taken “before the roots went onto glass.”

clues.title: The verge closing under direct light
clues.description: At the boundary itself, roots lift from salt and settle onto reflective glass with every pulse.

clues.title: Loaded east, empty west
clues.description: Every beetle entering the inner road bears a pellet. Every beetle returning along the margins is empty and turns back toward old ground.
clues.discovery: count both streams at a gate

clues.title: Pellets protected from spilled grain
clues.description: Soilbearers ignore exposed grain but cluster around dropped living-soil pellets and shield them from hooves.

clues.title: Five landscapes inside the mounds
clues.description: The carried ground contains distinct old ecologies preserved in small living parcels.

clues.title: Warm rain accepted only after soil delivery
clues.description: Root channels refuse water on pale untreated surfaces and open where delivered old ground has been mixed in.

clues.title: Crownward gates keyed to beetle vibration
clues.description: Inner root gates open for the cadence of laden beetle groups and close behind their soil.

clues.title: Knots filling after living-soil arrival
clues.description: Translucent crown knots begin clouding only when fresh old-ground mist reaches them.

clues.title: Bright pollen rising from delivered soil
clues.description: Lantern pollen activates only above roots darkened by living old ground and then travels crownward.

clues.title: Severed dawn has no road
clues.description: A fallen cup lights the bark around it, but no moth visits and no pollen filament leaves its cut stem.
clues.discovery: compare a fallen cup with a living opened flower

clues.title: Lit water entering the central branch
clues.description: Warm rain passing through open lantern stems carries bright pollen toward the crown.

clues.title: Dark knots beside a broken light thread
clues.description: Otherwise complete knots remain inert where lantern filaments fail to reach them.

clues.title: Mirror light does not wake a dark knot
clues.description: Direct sun floods the eastern crown, but a knot whose living dawn filament failed remains dark while a neighboring complete knot shines from within.
clues.discovery: compare two crown knots as direct sun reaches them

clues.title: A dry branch closing three lantern cups
clues.description: When one lower channel is pinched, several flowers close and the water later returns through a different basin.

clues.title: The mark comes home
clues.description: A mineral mark passes through root, fungus, lantern stem, and crown mist before returning cooler to the basin where it began.
clues.discovery: mark a measured cup and wait at the return

clues.title: The Bearer heating when flow is removed
clues.description: A temporarily blocked central channel raises the chamber temperature and shortens the preliminary breath.

clues.title: Returned water holds the boundary
clues.description: Two equal wet lines meet the advancing front. The line linked back to a basin stays cool and checks the flame; the poured line without a return steams dry and fails.
clues.discovery: compare a returned wet line with a poured boundary

clues.title: The basin answers the cloud
clues.description: A viable knot clouds when rain enters, then clears only when the same marked water appears cooler in its basin branch; a wet knot without that answer grows a white salt seam.
clues.discovery: watch the knot and its basin branch through one complete circuit

clues.title: Tovan's words without Tovan's answer
clues.description: The cords repeat Tovan's roster call but cannot respond when Hessa asks a question he would understand.

clues.title: One measurement in three voices
clues.description: The same flood depth appears in different languages and cadences as warm rain reaches separate cords.

clues.title: Kinship drifts; measure remains
clues.description: The same fragment keeps its slope and distance while a mother becomes a sister, then a stranger, across three repetitions.
clues.discovery: record three repetitions word for word

clues.title: Voice patterns aligned to water channels
